concepts.title: RSI(2) mean reversion
concepts.summary: Buy a stock that closes above its 200-day average when its 2-period RSI closes below 10 (usually after a sharp 2-3 day drop), and sell on the first close above the 5-day average. This lesson introduces the 'edge = conditional probability minus base rate' framing used throughout the course.

quantlab.hook: rsi_2 already exists: _rsi(c, 2) uses ewm(alpha=1/n), which matches Wilder's smoothing after a short warm-up. dist_sma_200 > 0 means a close above a 200-day SMA that needs only 100 days of history (min_periods=100), so below the rsi_2 line build connors_setup from c.rolling(200, min_periods=200) and add dist_sma_5 for the exit. Then delete data/cache/features_*.parquet (or run the CLI with --force), because the cache key ignores feature code and would silently hand you the old columns.

concepts.title: What 'the probability of a trade' means
concepts.summary: A probability is only meaningful once you define the trial (which day, which stock), the outcome (what counts as a win) and the horizon. Your model's p and a rule's hit rate answer different questions unless those three match.

quantlab.hook: make_labels turns every (date, ticker) row into a trial: with the defaults (threshold_sigma=0.30, horizon h=1), y=1 if fwd_ret > 0.30 x sigma x sqrt(h), y=0 if fwd_ret < -0.30 x sigma x sqrt(h), and NaN in the noise band between. Noise-band rows are dropped from training and calibration (drop_neutral=True) but kept in the backtests, so p estimates P(up | features, and the move left the band): not P(fwd_ret > 0), and not P(a multi-day trade ends in profit). If you change label.horizon, rebuild the features (the cache key ignores it), and remember both backtests treat fwd_ret as a 1-day return.

concepts.title: Base rates: the number every signal must beat
concepts.summary: Before praising any setup, measure how often the outcome happens anyway. If a stock rises on 54% of days regardless, a setup that wins 55% of the time adds almost nothing.

quantlab.hook: classification_metrics reports base_rate next to accuracy, and labels.label_summary gives positive_rate, but both are the share of y=1 among labelled rows, with the noise band removed. Before you look at any signal, compute P(fwd_ret > 0) from the features frame on all days and on days with dist_sma_200 > 0.

concepts.title: Expected value per trade
concepts.summary: EV = p x average win - (1 - p) x average loss - round-trip cost. This number, not the win rate, decides whether a rule makes money.

quantlab.hook: timing_summary reports hit_rate, trades and gross_ann_return but not EV per trade. 'trades' counts days with turnover, so a long-only round trip counts twice, and timing_backtest charges cost_bps on each side even though config.py calls it a round-trip cost. Group bt['position'] into trades and add avg_win, avg_loss and ev_per_round_trip net of 2 x cost_bps.

concepts.title: Hit rate versus payoff ratio
concepts.summary: A strategy can win 80% of the time and still lose money if its average loss is 5 times its average win (0.8 x 1 - 0.2 x 5 < 0). Mean-reversion rules often have a high hit rate and a low payoff ratio, while trend rules are often the reverse.

quantlab.hook: performance_summary reports only hit_rate, the share of days with a positive net return. Add the payoff ratio (average gain / average loss) and the profit factor (total gains / total losses). timing_summary's hit_rate is also per day and counts days out of the market as non-wins, so it is not a per-trade hit rate.

concepts.title: Calibration: does 60% really mean 60%?
concepts.summary: A model can rank days correctly but still state the wrong probabilities. Calibration remaps its scores so that, among all the days it calls 60%, the event happens on about 60%.

quantlab.hook: Calibrator('sigmoid'), the config default, is Platt scaling: a logistic regression on the model's log-odds, fit only on the inner validation block. reliability_curve returns (mean predicted, observed frequency, count) per bin and expected_calibration_error averages the gap; pass only rows where y is not NaN, or the noise-band rows turn the result into NaN. The module docstring explains why isotonic was rejected.

concepts.title: Brier score and Brier skill
concepts.summary: The Brier score is the mean squared error of probabilities. Brier skill compares it with always predicting the base rate, so skill <= 0 means your probabilities add nothing.

quantlab.hook: classification_metrics computes brier and brier_skill = 1 - brier / brier_base, where brier_base is the error of always predicting that sample's own base rate. run_walk_forward in train.py records brier_skill (on the calibrated p) for every fold in fold_metrics.csv, so check whether it is positive in most folds. Because the base rate is measured on the test fold itself, this benchmark is slightly harder to beat than any rate you could have known in advance.

concepts.title: Sample size: how many trades before you believe it
concepts.summary: A hit rate measured on N independent trades has standard error sqrt(p(1-p)/N). With 100 trades and a hit rate near 50-60%, the 95% interval is about +/- 10 points, so most short-term setups need hundreds of trades.

quantlab.hook: performance_summary reports t_stat = mean daily net return / its standard error, and its comment says that below ~2 the edge cannot be told apart from luck. timing_summary has no t_stat, so compute it from bt['net_return'] for a single-name run. For your RSI(2) trade list, test the hit rate against the base rate with sqrt(p(1-p)/N), and remember that trades on different stocks on the same day are not independent.

concepts.title: Z-score and Bollinger %b mean reversion
concepts.summary: Measure how far price is from its recent average in units of its recent standard deviation, and bet on a return toward the average when that distance is extreme. It is a close cousin of RSI(2), measured on a different scale.

quantlab.hook: _z(x, window) is a trailing z-score (min_periods = window // 2), and bollinger_pctb = (c - 20d mean) / (2 x 20d std), so _z(c, 20) is exactly 2 x bollinger_pctb. That is a rescaled %b: -1 is the lower band and +1 the upper band, whereas the standard %b runs from 0 to 1. Test 'buy when bollinger_pctb < -1 and dist_sma_200 > 0' with the same base-rate comparison you used for RSI(2).

concepts.title: IBS: internal bar strength
concepts.summary: IBS = (close - low) / (high - low) says where today's close sits in today's range. Practitioner studies of equity ETFs found that closes near the low (IBS < 0.2) tended to precede next-day gains, but the published evidence is thin, so you must test it yourself net of costs.

quantlab.hook: close_loc_value = (c - l) / (h - l + EPS) is exactly IBS; the back-adjustment scales h, l and c by the same factor, so the ratio is unchanged. Bucket it into quintiles and compare P(fwd_ret > 0) per bucket with the base rate, then check how often close_loc_value < 0.2 coincides with rsi_2 < 10. The published tests used ETFs, so do not assume the effect carries over to single stocks.

concepts.title: Streaks: consecutive down days
concepts.summary: Counting consecutive down closes is the crudest oversold measure. It overlaps heavily with RSI(2), which teaches you that many 'different' signals are really the same signal.

quantlab.hook: _streak builds the streak column: the signed length of the current run of up (+) or down (-) closes, clipped at +/-10, with a flat day resetting it to 0. Compare P(up next day | streak <= -3) with P(up next day | rsi_2 < 10), and measure their correlation and how often both fire on the same day.

concepts.title: Trend filters: the 200-day moving average
concepts.summary: Trading only in the direction of the long-term average aims to avoid buying dips inside bear markets, at the cost of lag: the filter flips only after much of a decline has happened.

quantlab.hook: dist_sma_200 is the log distance from the 200-day SMA divided by volatility, so only its sign means above or below, and min_periods=100 means early values average fewer than 200 days. cross_sectional.build_market adds mkt_dist_sma_200, the same idea for an equal-weighted index of your panel (not the S&P 500), and single-name mode drops it as meaningless.

concepts.title: Time-series momentum
concepts.summary: Time-series momentum bets that an asset's own past trend continues: long when its past 12-month return is positive, short or in cash when it is negative. The best evidence is in diversified futures; for a single stock, the long-or-cash version mainly aims to sit out long declines, at the cost of lag and whipsaw losses.

quantlab.hook: mom_252_21 and mom_126_21 are log returns from 252 (or 126) days ago to 21 days ago, divided by daily volatility, so their sign is the past trend with the latest month skipped (the classic signal uses the full 12 months). To score 'hold if mom_252_21 > 0', put (mom_252_21 > 0) in a p column next to fwd_ret for one ticker, keep the (date, ticker) index, and call timing.timing_backtest(preds, cfg.backtest). Drop the first year, where mom_252_21 is NaN, or that warm-up counts as time out of the market against buy-and-hold.

concepts.title: Cross-sectional momentum and the skip month
concepts.summary: Rank stocks against each other by past 12-month return, buy the leaders and, in the classic version, short the laggards. The most recent month is skipped because one-month returns have tended to reverse instead.

quantlab.hook: RANKED includes mom_252_21, so cs_rank_mom_252_21 is each stock's daily percentile among its peers; because mom_252_21 is divided by volatility, this ranks risk-adjusted momentum, not raw 12-month return. For a pure momentum book, join that column into the predictions frame and call backtest.engine.run_backtest(preds, cfg.backtest, score_col='cs_rank_mom_252_21'): build_weights alone returns only weights, and it takes no positions on days with fewer than 20 names.

concepts.title: Why the sign flips: 1-day reversal versus 12-month momentum
concepts.summary: Across US stocks, returns have tended to reverse over days to a month and to continue over roughly 3-12 months. Choosing the horizon is choosing the strategy family.

quantlab.hook: rev_1d, rev_5d and rev_21d are negated, volatility-scaled returns (rev_1d is just -ret_1d / vol_21), while mom_* keep the positive sign; the README calls reversal 'the strongest genuine 1-day equity effect'. feature_importance in models/base.py reports only |coef|, so fit a LogisticModel yourself on labelled rows and read model.pipe[-1].coef_[0]; the quantile transform is monotone, so signs survive. ret_1d, rev_1d and their cs_ versions are near-duplicates, so one coefficient's sign can mislead: check one feature at a time, for example P(y=1) by rev_1d quintile.

concepts.title: Gap behaviour: overnight versus intraday returns
concepts.summary: A day's return splits into the overnight gap (previous close to open) and the session (open to close). The two parts behave differently: several studies of US stocks found that much of the long-run gain came overnight, though this varies by period and market.

quantlab.hook: overnight_ret (identical to gap_open) and intraday_ret are divided by vol_21, so they are in volatility units. On the same row, check whether a gap below -2 is followed by intraday_ret > 0 more often than on all days. The pipeline's label and backtests run close to close, so a trade entered at the open needs its own open-to-close P&L.

concepts.title: Seasonality: the turn-of-the-month effect
concepts.summary: US index returns have historically clustered in the last trading day and first three trading days of each month; one study found that over 1926-2005 the average market premium came only in that window. The cause is still debated, and calendar effects are easy to find by data mining, so be sceptical.

quantlab.hook: calendar_features builds is_month_end (within 2 calendar days of the month's last day) and is_month_start (calendar day 1 to 3, which can be a single trading day after a weekend). They are the same for every stock on a date, so on their own they cannot change the cross-sectional ranking (a tree model can use them only through interactions). In single-name mode, compare the share of y = 1 on flagged rows with the base rate, remembering that row t's label is the next day's return.

concepts.title: Mean-reversion half-life (Ornstein-Uhlenbeck)
concepts.summary: Model a price's deviation from its mean as an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process. Regressing the daily change on the lagged level gives a slope b, and half-life = -ln(2)/b (approximately, for small negative b) estimates how long a typical gap takes to halve, a guide to how long to hold.

quantlab.hook: autocorr_21 is the lag-1 autocorrelation of daily returns over a rolling 63-day window, despite its name, and a negative value hints at mean reversion. If you add a rolling half-life feature (regress the change in log price on its lagged level, keep only b < 0), first run it on a simulated random walk: 63-day windows report half-lives of about 10 days from pure noise, and a distance-to-SMA series reverts by construction. Then delete data/cache/features_*.parquet, because the feature cache does not notice code changes.

concepts.title: Pairs trading and cointegration
concepts.summary: Two related prices can each wander while their spread stays mean-reverting (cointegrated). You trade the spread, not either stock alone, but only after testing that it is stationary, and a relationship that held in the past can break.

quantlab.hook: build_beta regresses each stock's daily log return on the equal-weight average return over a rolling 63 days to get beta_63, and idio_ret_1d is that day's residual divided by its own EWMA volatility. A pair trade works on price levels instead: regress one log price on the other on training dates to get a hedge ratio, then test the spread with an Engle-Granger test (statsmodels' coint, which is not in requirements.txt). A residual of returns such as idio_ret_1d is almost always stationary, so testing it says nothing about the pair.

concepts.title: Measuring volatility: EWMA and range estimators
concepts.summary: Most sizing and labelling rules need a volatility estimate. EWMA weights recent days more heavily, and high-low range estimators use intraday information that the close throws away, but they miss the overnight gap.

quantlab.hook: realised_vol is the causal EWMA standard deviation of daily log returns that scales the label (vol_halflife = 21), and vol_21 in technical.py is the same number; vol_10 and vol_63 are EWMAs with halflives 10 and 63, while parkinson_21 and garman_klass_21 are 21-day range averages. Compare them on a calm and a volatile year. Expect the range estimators to read lower than vol_21 on stocks with big overnight gaps, because they see only the trading session.

concepts.title: Volatility targeting
concepts.summary: Scale position size by target volatility / forecast volatility, so the strategy takes similar risk in calm and stormy markets. Studies have found this tends to raise Sharpe and cut extreme losses for equities, with little Sharpe gain in bonds or currencies, and it is not guaranteed for every asset or period.

quantlab.hook: timing_backtest sets pos = 1 whenever p > threshold. preds from run_walk_forward carries sigma (the label's EWMA daily volatility), but timing_backtest keeps only date, p and fwd_ret, so in your copy keep sigma and set pos = min(1, target_daily_vol / sigma) on days it would hold (0.01 a day is about 16% a year). Compare Sharpe and max_drawdown in timing_summary with the 0/1 version, remembering that resizing every day adds turnover and cost and inflates the trades count.

concepts.title: Position sizing and the Kelly criterion
concepts.summary: For a bet that wins b times the stake with probability p and otherwise loses the whole stake, the Kelly fraction f* = p - (1 - p)/b maximises long-run growth when p and b are known exactly. Betting more than Kelly lowers growth: at about twice Kelly, growth falls to roughly zero, and beyond that capital shrinks.

quantlab.hook: A day in the stock does not lose its whole stake, so with average win W and average loss L (as fractions) the Kelly position is p/L - (1 - p)/W; clip it to between 0 and 1 and use it as pos in a copy of timing_backtest. Your calibrated p is the chance of a move above +0.3 sigma on days outside the dropped noise band, so take W and L as the average simple return on y = 1 and y = 0 days in training data, not on the days you score. With W and L near 1%, p = 0.52 already asks for 4x leverage, which is why you cap it.

concepts.title: Why fractional Kelly
concepts.summary: Kelly assumes your p is correct, but an estimated p is always noisy and often optimistic, because you act on the bets where it looks best. In the standard continuous approximation, half-Kelly keeps about three-quarters of full Kelly's growth rate with half the volatility, and it is much more robust to an overstated edge.

quantlab.hook: expected_calibration_error is the average gap between predicted and observed probability across 20 equal-count bins, in either direction, and fold_metrics reports it per fold as ece_calibrated. As a crude, conservative haircut, take p minus the ECE from earlier folds, recompute the Kelly position, and see how much of the bet survives. With only a few hundred test days, much of the ECE is sampling noise, so this haircut is harsh.

concepts.title: Risk of ruin and drawdowns
concepts.summary: Risk of ruin is the probability that a sequence of losses takes you below a level you can't recover from, financially or psychologically. It rises steeply with bet size and, at the same hit rate, with a lower payoff ratio.

quantlab.hook: _stats computes max_drawdown from the equity curve. timing_summary's hit_rate counts every day, including days out of the market, so work out the hit rate and payoff ratio over days with position = 1 only. Then simulate many sequences at 1x, 0.5x and 0.25x size and count how often equity falls 30% below its peak; resampling your real in-market daily returns in blocks keeps the fat tails and volatility clusters that a two-outcome model misses.

concepts.title: Transaction costs and slippage
concepts.summary: Spread, commission, slippage against your intended price and market impact are paid on every trade. Short-horizon strategies earn small amounts per trade, so costs decide whether they survive.

quantlab.hook: run_backtest charges cost = turnover x cost_bps / 1e4, and cost_sensitivity reruns it at 0, 2, 5, 10 and 20 bps. Turnover counts both the buy and the sell, so a full round trip pays cost_bps twice, even though config.py calls it a round-trip cost. The module docstring lists what is not modelled (impact beyond a flat spread, borrow costs, slippage against the close, capacity), and each of these makes results worse.

concepts.title: Turnover and the breakeven cost
concepts.summary: Breakeven cost = average gross return / average turnover: the cost per unit traded (each buy or sell) at which profit falls to zero. If it is below what you really pay per trade, the strategy is not tradeable.

quantlab.hook: _breakeven_cost_bps implements this, the README calls the breakeven cost the most valuable output of the repo, and timing_summary reports the same as breakeven_cost_bps for the single-name book. Because turnover counts each buy and each sell, compare it with your one-way cost (half the bid-ask spread plus commission and slippage), not a round-trip cost. Compare RSI(2), which trades only occasionally, with the daily model, which can change position much more often.

concepts.title: Sharpe, Sortino, max drawdown and Calmar
concepts.summary: Sharpe divides return by total volatility, while Sortino uses only downside volatility. Max drawdown is the worst peak-to-trough loss, and Calmar is annual return divided by that drawdown; each one hides something the others reveal.

quantlab.hook: performance_summary has sharpe, max_drawdown and calmar but no Sortino, and it also runs on timing_backtest output, which has the same net_return, gross_return, turnover and cost columns. Add sortino = mean x 252 / (downside deviation x sqrt(252)), where downside deviation = sqrt(mean(min(r, 0)^2)) over all days. A symmetric book scores a Sortino about 1.4 times its Sharpe, so a lower ratio in a mean-reversion book points to a fat left tail.

concepts.title: The right benchmark: buy-and-hold for a single stock
concepts.summary: A timing rule for one stock must beat simply holding it, and on a risk-adjusted basis. A rule that is invested 20% of the time also has to be judged per unit of exposure.

quantlab.hook: timing_summary reports excess_ann_return, excess_sharpe and time_in_market, and timing_verdict says BEAT only when excess Sharpe > 0.3 and excess return > 0. Also compute strategy_ann_return / time_in_market, the return per unit of exposure, and compare it with buy_hold_ann_return. Days out of the market earn 0 here, with no interest on cash.

concepts.title: Look-ahead bias
concepts.summary: Look-ahead bias means using any information that was not available at the moment of the decision. Common examples are centred moving averages, same-day closes used for an open entry, and revised data; it produces backtests that cannot be traded.

quantlab.hook: The main test rebuilds every feature on the synthetic panel from tests/conftest.py (not your upload) cut off about 120 trading days early, and fails if any value on a shared date changes. Run pytest tests/test_no_lookahead.py after adding dist_sma_5 and connors_setup; a deliberately centred mean such as c.rolling(5, center=True).mean() added to build_technical should make it fail. It checks features only, so labels (which look forward by design) and survivorship bias are outside its reach.

concepts.title: Survivorship bias
concepts.summary: Testing on today's index members leaves out firms that went bankrupt, were bought out or were dropped, and includes others only because they later grew. Dip-buying rules are flattered in particular, because in a survivors-only list every dip you 'bought' was in a company that lived on.

quantlab.hook: default_universe is a bundled list of today's S&P 500 members, and with source='yahoo' only those names (plus SPY, QQQ and IWM) are downloaded, so delisted firms never enter your panel. apply_membership(panel, load_membership(csv)) keeps only point-in-time members, but nothing in the pipeline calls it (the --universe-file flag in its docstring does not exist), and it cannot add names you have no prices for, so you would also need delisted firms' price files, for example through the upload source.

concepts.title: Purged k-fold and embargo
concepts.summary: When a label looks h days ahead, training rows just before the test period already contain part of its outcome. Purging removes training rows whose label window overlaps the test period, and the embargo also drops training rows just after each test block, because dependence can outlast the label.

quantlab.hook: purged_walk_forward splits on dates and leaves a fixed gap of purge_days + embargo_days (default 5 + 10 trading days) before each test block, and the same gap between inner-train and inner-val; that gap is the purge, rather than a row-by-row check. validate_config rejects purge_days < label.horizon, so a 5-day label needs a purge of at least 5, and because training never comes after a test block here, the embargo simply widens the gap.

concepts.title: Walk-forward analysis
concepts.summary: Train on the past, test on the next block, roll forward and repeat. It mimics trading in real time and shows performance period by period, but only if you did not choose settings after seeing the test results.

quantlab.hook: run_walk_forward trains on each fold, calibrates on inner_val and scores each test block once; fold_metrics (saved as fold_metrics.csv) records daily_auc, auc, brier_skill, ece_raw and ece_calibrated per period, and daily_auc is NaN when a date has fewer than 20 labelled names. A fold with too few labelled rows is skipped with only a log warning, so count the rows and read the fold table, not just the pooled result.

concepts.title: Overfitting and the simple-model control
concepts.summary: More flexible models and more rules fit noise more easily. The cheapest guard is to demand that any complex approach beat a simple one on identical data and splits.

quantlab.hook: run_everything (compare_baseline=True by default) fits the logistic control on the same data and folds, and summarize warns unless boosting beats it by more than 0.002 AUC (within-date AUC for a panel, pooled AUC for one stock); that margin is a rule of thumb, not a significance test. For a trading rule, the matching control is buy-and-hold, or the 200-day filter on its own.

concepts.title: Multiple testing: deflated Sharpe and PBO
concepts.summary: The best of many backtests is biased upward. The deflated Sharpe ratio gives the probability that the best Sharpe reflects real skill after allowing for the number of variants tried, skew, fat tails and sample length, and the probability of backtest overfitting (PBO) estimates how often the in-sample winner lands at or below the median out of sample.

quantlab.hook: performance_summary gives Sharpe and t_stat for one run only, with no allowance for the other variants you tried. Save the daily net_return of every variant (threshold, exit, filter, model): the deflated Sharpe needs the number of trials, how much their Sharpes varied, and the winner's daily (not annualised) Sharpe, skew, kurtosis and number of days.

concepts.title: Regime dependence
concepts.summary: Edges change with volatility, trend and liquidity regimes. A rule that only works in calm bull markets is a regime bet, and you need to know that before the regime changes.

quantlab.hook: build_market makes mkt_vol_z, mkt_drawdown and mkt_dist_sma_200 from the equal-weight average of the panel, but in single-name mode (fewer than 20 names) run_everything drops them, since for one stock they are just the stock itself. So split your RSI(2) trades by the stock's own vol_z_252 and drawdown_252, or use a panel, and compare net return per trade in each regime; easy._caveats already warns when AUC is above 0.505 in at most one test fold.

concepts.title: Monte Carlo and the bootstrap of trades
concepts.summary: One backtest is one path. Resampling its trades, or blocks of days, thousands of times gives a range of returns and drawdowns that shows how much of the result could be luck, though it cannot fix a biased or overfitted backtest.

quantlab.hook: timing_backtest returns a daily net_return (0 on days out of the market); run_everything already gives it to you as bundle['results']['timing_bt'] in single-name mode, and a panel run has bundle['results']['bt_series']. Resample it in blocks (say 20 days, so calm and stormy stretches stay together) 5,000 times, and report the 5th percentile of annual return and of max drawdown (drawdowns are negative numbers here, so the 5th percentile is the bad tail).

concepts.title: Label design: horizon and volatility scaling
concepts.summary: The label defines what the model learns. A fixed 1-day sign label, a volatility-scaled label with a dropped noise band, and a multi-day label each ask a different question.

quantlab.hook: make_labels sets the noise band at threshold_sigma x sigma x sqrt(h) and drops the rows inside it (check positive_rate in label_summary). easy.run_everything has no horizon option, so set label.horizon (3-5) in a copy of configs/default.yaml, keep split.purge_days >= horizon, and run python -m quantlab.cli run --config <your copy> --force, since the feature cache key ignores label.horizon. With h > 1, fwd_ret overlaps from day to day, so the backtest, the decile ann_return and the t-stats all overstate: trust only the AUC and IC values.

concepts.title: Triple-barrier labels
concepts.summary: A trade ends at whichever comes first: a profit target, a stop-loss or a time limit. Labelling each day by which of these barriers is hit first matches how a trade with a target and a stop really ends, unlike a label that looks at one fixed future day.

quantlab.hook: make_labels looks only at the close h days ahead. Write make_triple_barrier_labels beside it (barriers at +/- k x sigma x sqrt(h), time limit h days), use its y in features/build.build_features, and add any extra column it returns, such as the exit day, to META_COLS, or the model trains on the future. Keep label.horizon = 1 so fwd_ret stays a one-day return, raise split.purge_days to at least h yourself (validate_config checks only label.horizon), and delete data/cache, which holds the old labels.

concepts.title: Meta-labeling
concepts.summary: Let a simple rule decide the direction and timing, then train a model only to predict whether that rule's trade will succeed, and use its probability to take, skip or size the trade.

quantlab.hook: connors_setup is not in the code yet (you add it to features/technical.py for RSI(2)), and after adding it you must delete data/cache, because the feature cache key ignores code changes. Keep only setup rows, set y to whether the rule's own round trip made money after costs, raise split.purge_days to your longest trade, and pool many tickers, since run_walk_forward skips any fold with under 250 labelled training rows and min_train_days counts only the dates left. Score it as average net return per trade taken versus all setups, not with timing_backtest, which treats each row as one day.

concepts.title: Feature importance pitfalls
concepts.summary: Importance shows what the model used, not what is true or causal. Correlated features split the credit, and market-wide features can rank high without improving stock selection.

quantlab.hook: importance is LightGBM gain from each fold's training fit, normalised per fold and averaged, so it can reward features that only fit noise. ret_1d, rev_1d, their cs_rank_ and cs_z_ versions and idio_ret_1d all encode the last day's move (and overlap with rsi_2), so they split the credit; easy._caveats warns when at least 3 of the top 5 features are market-wide (mkt_*, breadth_*, cs_dispersion*, avg_corr_proxy).

concepts.title: Probability thresholds and EV per trade
concepts.summary: Trading whenever p > 0.5 ignores costs and the sizes of wins and losses. The threshold should be where expected value per trade after costs turns positive, and you must choose it without looking at the data you test it on.

quantlab.hook: timing_backtest(threshold=0.5) holds the stock on every day the calibrated p is above 0.5, and BacktestConfig.min_probability adds a floor to the cross-sectional book (a top-ranked name is bought only if p >= min_probability, a bottom-ranked one shorted only if p <= 1 - min_probability). run_walk_forward does not save its inner-validation predictions, so choose the threshold on the early folds only (for example folds 0-1) and judge it on the later ones.

concepts.title: Combining signals
concepts.summary: Several weak, partly independent signals can be combined into a stronger one by averaging their z-scores, by a linear model or by a tree model. The more correlated the signals are, the less you gain.

quantlab.hook: LogisticModel is a median imputer, a QuantileTransformer to a normal shape and a logistic regression with C=0.05 (strong regularisation), the simplest learned combiner. As an unfitted control, z-score rsi_2, close_loc_value and streak yourself (they have no cs_z_ columns), average them and flip the sign, since low values are the bullish ones. Score it on the same out-of-sample rows with metrics.mean_daily_auc for a panel or sklearn's roc_auc_score for one stock, not classification_metrics, which clips scores into 0-1.

concepts.title: Paper trading discipline
concepts.summary: Before risking money, record each signal before the market opens and compare the live results with the backtest. The gap shows the costs, delays and biases the backtest missed.

quantlab.hook: predict_latest refits on all history and scores the newest date in your data, and easy.run_everything writes it to tomorrow_predictions.csv, overwriting the last one. With source='yahoo' the prices are cached under a key that ignores today's date, so call pipeline.predict_latest(cfg, force=True) and check the date before you archive each day's file. The backtest assumes you trade at the signal day's close, so log the price you could really get, and after about 3 months compare live results with the walk-forward ones.

note: Quant strategy curriculum; one concept per morning, tied to quant-lab files. Two independent verification passes.
